input:
Priya: Quick one before we close. The nightly Magpie ingest has been finishing at 06:40 instead of 05:00 for a week now, so the dashboards are stale when the first customers log in.
Tomasz: I looked at it yesterday. The slow part is the dedup step. It does a full table scan since the partition change went in.
Lena: Can we put the partition key back on the dedup query? That is what it used to do before the change.
Tomasz: Yes. About a day of work plus a backfill check to make sure nothing was double counted while it was slow.
Priya: Okay. Tomasz owns adding the partition key back to the dedup step, target is end of this week, with the backfill check included.
Tomasz: Fine by me.
Lena: Unrelated, did anyone else lose badge access on the fourth floor this morning? The reader flashed red at me twice and I had to wait for someone to let me in.
Priya: Mine worked. Ask facilities, I think they re-imaged the readers over the weekend.
Lena: Will do. Sorry, back to the ingest.
Priya: Nothing more on it. Tomasz, post in the channel when the backfill check is done so support knows the numbers are trustworthy again.
Tomasz: Will do.
output: The nightly Magpie ingest is slow because the dedup step lost its partition key after the partition change, so Tomasz will add the partition key back to the dedup query and run a backfill check by the end of the week. He will post in the channel when the backfill check is done.

input:
Mei: Support has three tickets this week about the Perch CSV export. Customers open it in a spreadsheet and every accented name comes out as garbage characters.
Rafael: That is the encoding. We write UTF-8 without a byte order mark, and the spreadsheet tools guess Latin-1 when the mark is missing.
Zoe: Is adding the mark safe for the customers who load the file into their own pipelines? Some of them parse it with scripts.
Rafael: Every parser we have seen handles the mark. I checked the two biggest customers' import scripts last quarter for the same reason.
Mei: Then let's do it. Rafael, you own switching the CSV export to write the byte order mark, and please add a note in the export dialog so nobody is surprised.
Rafael: I can have it in the Thursday release.
Zoe: Totally different topic, the coffee machine on this floor now asks for a pin code. Does anyone know it?
Mei: It is the same as the meeting room code. Someone taped it under the tray.
Zoe: Thanks, I was about to walk to the second floor for every cup.
Mei: Right, back to work. Rafael, ping me when the export change is in review and I will reply to the tickets.
output: Accented characters in the Perch CSV export are corrupted in spreadsheets because the file is written without a byte order mark. Rafael will switch the export to write the byte order mark and add a note in the export dialog, targeting the Thursday release.

input:
Jonas: The Kestrel query timeout is biting the two enterprise tenants again. Their month-end reports run for about forty seconds and we cut them off at thirty.
Hana: We set thirty deliberately so a runaway query could not hold a worker for long. Raising it means fewer workers free at peak.
Kofi: Peak is not month end though. The long reports run on the first two days of the month, when interactive traffic is at its lowest.
Jonas: And the alternative is telling those tenants to split their reports by hand, which they will not do.
Hana: Fine. If we raise it, we raise it to sixty and no higher, and we keep the per-tenant concurrency cap where it is.
Jonas: Agreed. Hana, you own raising the Kestrel query timeout from thirty to sixty seconds. Ship it before the first of the month.
Hana: I will put it behind the usual config change and watch the worker pool for a day.
Kofi: On another note, I finished the half marathon on Sunday. Two hours and eleven minutes, so not fast, but I did not walk.
Jonas: Nice. Was that the one along the river?
Kofi: Yes, the route with the terrible hill at kilometre eighteen.
Jonas: Okay, that is the timeout settled. Nothing else from me.
output: Enterprise month-end reports are being cut off by Kestrel's thirty-second query timeout, so Hana will raise the timeout from thirty to sixty seconds before the first of the month. The per-tenant concurrency cap stays as it is.

input:
Nadia: Talon still serves the v1 webhook format, and the last time I checked only four tenants use it. Everyone else moved to v2 last year.
Theo: Four tenants is still four tenants. If we just switch it off, they find out when their alerts stop arriving.
Amara: Nobody is proposing switching it off tomorrow. The question is whether we announce a date.
Nadia: I think we should. Ninety days notice, with a migration guide and a direct mail to the four tenant admins.
Theo: Ninety days is fair. Who writes the notice?
Nadia: I will. I own the deprecation notice for the v1 webhook, with a ninety-day window, and it goes out Thursday.
Amara: Copy the account managers so they are not surprised by replies.
Nadia: Will do.
Theo: Different thing entirely, the parking garage is closing the lower level for repainting next week. If you park down there you will need to use the street lot.
Amara: For how long?
Theo: They said two weeks, which probably means three.
Nadia: Noted. Back to it. I will circulate the notice draft tomorrow so you can both read it before it goes out.
output: Only four tenants still use Talon's v1 webhook format, so it will be deprecated with a ninety-day window. Nadia will write and send the deprecation notice on Thursday, with a migration guide and the account managers copied.

input:
Marcus: Our on-call rotation is daily, and the handover every morning is where things get dropped. Twice last month an open incident was not mentioned at handover at all.
Elin: Weekly would fix the handover problem but a bad week is a very long week for whoever has the pager.
Dario: Most teams I have been on ran weekly with a secondary. The secondary takes over if the primary has had two nights disturbed.
Marcus: That is what I want to propose. Weekly primary, weekly secondary, offset by half a week so they do not both start fresh on the same day.
Elin: I can live with that if the secondary rule is written down and not just understood.
Marcus: It will be. Dario, can you own updating the schedule tool to the weekly rotation with the offset secondary?
Dario: Yes. I will move it over at the start of next month so the current schedule is not disturbed.
Elin: Did anybody water the plants in the corner office? The big one is drooping and I think it has been three weeks.
Marcus: I thought that was your plant.
Elin: It is nobody's plant, which is the problem.
Marcus: I will water it on the way out. Right, weekly rotation, Dario has it, done.
output: The on-call rotation moves from daily to weekly, with a weekly secondary offset by half a week and the secondary rule written down. Dario will update the schedule tool to the new rotation at the start of next month.

input:
Ingrid: Two customers asked for longer history in Rookery. We keep ninety days of raw events and they want to run half-year comparisons.
Amara: Doubling retention doubles the raw storage, roughly. It is not a small line item.
Ravi: Only if we keep the raw tier at full resolution. Aggregates are already kept for two years, it is only the raw events that roll off.
Ingrid: The half-year comparisons need the raw events, they filter by fields we do not aggregate.
Amara: Then I want a real number before we commit. Let me pull the current raw volume and price a hundred and eighty days at the cold tier rate.
Ingrid: That is fair. Amara owns producing the storage estimate for a hundred and eighty days of raw retention, and we decide on the change once we have it.
Amara: I will have it by Friday.
Ravi: Has anyone tried the new noodle place across the road? The queue at noon was out the door.
Ingrid: I went Monday. Good, but the portions are enormous, get the small one.
Ravi: Noted.
Ingrid: Okay, Amara has the estimate, and we revisit retention when it lands.
output: Two customers want longer raw event history in Rookery than the current ninety days. Amara will produce a storage estimate for a hundred and eighty days of raw retention by Friday, and the retention change itself will be decided once the estimate is in.

input:
Theo: The CI queue is forty minutes deep most afternoons. Half the builds are waiting on a runner rather than actually running.
Felix: We are on the small runner class. The build itself is eight minutes, the wait is thirty.
Sofia: What does the larger class cost? I remember looking at this last year and it was about double.
Felix: It is about double per runner, but we would need half as many, because the compile step scales with cores and it is most of the build.
Theo: So roughly cost neutral and the queue goes away. Felix, you own moving the CI runners to the larger instance class. Do it on a Monday morning so we are around if it misbehaves.
Felix: I will do next Monday and keep the old pool warm for a day as a fallback.
Sofia: Did either of you watch the recording of that talk on incremental compilation from the conference last month? The speaker got a large build down to under a minute.
Theo: I saw the slides. Most of it depended on their build tool, which we do not use.
Sofia: Still worth a look for the caching part.
Theo: Send the link. Anyway, runners: Felix, Monday, larger class. That is it for me.
output: The CI queue is long because builds wait on the small runner class, so the runners move to the larger instance class. Felix will make the move next Monday, keeping the old pool warm for a day as a fallback.

input:
Leila: User research keeps flagging the word workspace in Perch. Customers call the same thing a project, and the sales deck calls it a project, so the product is the odd one out.
Ben: Renaming a core noun touches every screen, the docs, and the exported reports.
Zoe: The API can keep calling it workspace though. Nobody is asking to break integrations, only the visible copy.
Leila: Exactly. UI copy and the docs, nothing in the API, nothing in the database.
Ben: If it is only the copy layer it is a couple of days. I would want one review pass so we do not end up with both words on the same screen.
Leila: Agreed. Ben, you own renaming workspace to project across the Perch UI copy and docs, with the API untouched, by the end of the sprint.
Ben: Okay.
Zoe: My cat has learned to open the cupboard where the food is, so I now have a cat that is fifteen percent larger than last month.
Leila: Child lock?
Zoe: Ordered one this morning.
Leila: Good luck. Ben, ping me for the review pass when the rename is ready.
output: The Perch UI will stop saying workspace and say project instead, matching what customers and the sales deck call it, while the API and database keep the old name. Ben will make the rename across the UI copy and docs by the end of the sprint, with one review pass before it ships.

input:
Kofi: One tenant's script hammered the public metrics endpoint at about three thousand requests a minute last night. It was not malicious, it was a retry loop with no backoff, but it slowed everyone else down.
Yara: We have no rate limit on that endpoint at all, do we?
Kofi: None. Every other public endpoint has one, this was missed when it launched.
Viktor: What is a fair limit? The heaviest legitimate user I know of polls once a second.
Kofi: Six hundred a minute gives ten per second, so ten times the heaviest real usage, and it still would have stopped last night's loop.
Yara: And we return the standard too-many-requests response with the retry header so well-behaved clients slow down on their own.
Kofi: Yes. I own adding a six hundred per minute per tenant rate limit to the public metrics endpoint, same middleware as the other endpoints. It ships this week.
Viktor: Good. On a completely different subject, my laptop battery now lasts about forty minutes. Is there a form for that or do I just ask?
Yara: There is a form. Search the help desk for battery replacement and it comes up.
Viktor: Thanks.
Kofi: Nothing else from me, the rate limit is the only item.
output: A tenant's retry loop overloaded the public metrics endpoint, which has no rate limit. Kofi will add a six hundred requests per minute per tenant rate limit this week, using the same middleware as the other public endpoints.

input:
Ingrid: The Rookery schema migration was planned for this sprint, but the two people who know the migration tool best are both out next week.
Dev: I could run it alone, but if it goes wrong at step four I would be guessing, and it is a migration of the largest table we have.
Sofia: The customer commitment was for the quarter, not for this sprint. Nobody outside this room is waiting on it this week.
Ingrid: Then I would rather move it. One sprint later with both experts present beats this sprint with one.
Dev: Agreed. And it gives me time to run the dry run against the staging copy first, which we skipped in the plan.
Ingrid: Then it is decided, the migration moves to next sprint. I own updating the roadmap and telling the account team about the new date.
Sofia: Thanks. Are the trains going to be running Thursday? My app says strike but the operator's page says nothing.
Dev: The strike is only the regional lines, I think. The express should be fine.
Sofia: I will leave early anyway.
Ingrid: Sensible. Okay, migration is next sprint, roadmap update is mine, we are done.
output: The Rookery schema migration is postponed from this sprint to the next one so both migration experts are present and a staging dry run can happen first. Ingrid will update the roadmap and tell the account team the new date.

input:
Sofia: The Magpie fetch from object storage failed eleven times yesterday. Every failure was a transient network error and every one of them dropped the batch on the floor.
Dev: We never added a retry there. The fetch is a single call with a single try.
Priya: And nobody knew until the morning, because nothing alerts on ingest lag, only on outright job failure, and the job did not fail, it just skipped batches.
Sofia: Two things, then. Retry the fetch, and alert on lag.
Dev: I can add a retry with exponential backoff, three attempts, on the fetch call. That covers the transient errors.
Sofia: Okay, Dev owns the retry with backoff on the object storage fetch.
Priya: And I will add a Talon alert when ingest lag goes over thirty minutes, routed to the data on-call. That would have paged at about two in the morning yesterday, which is what we want.
Sofia: Good. Priya owns the lag alert at thirty minutes.
Dev: Has anyone found a venue for the team offsite? The place by the lake wants a deposit by Friday and I do not think anyone has looked at alternatives.
Priya: I looked at two. Both were worse. Let's just pay the deposit.
Dev: Fine, I will tell them.
Sofia: Right. Retry is Dev's, lag alert is Priya's, both this week please.
output: Magpie's object storage fetch drops batches on transient errors, so Dev will add a three-attempt retry with exponential backoff on the fetch call. Priya will add a Talon alert that pages the data on-call when ingest lag exceeds thirty minutes, and both changes are due this week.

input:
Hana: The slow query report from last week is almost entirely joins between two large tables where Kestrel picked a nested loop. Every one of those would be faster as a hash join.
Viktor: The planner picks nested loop when it thinks one side is small, and the statistics for those tables are stale.
Rafael: Refreshing statistics is a treadmill. We could just default to hash join once both sides are over ten million rows, regardless of what the estimates say.
Hana: That is what I want. Above ten million rows on both sides, hash join by default. I own making that planner change and running it against the slow query set before it ships.
Viktor: Fine, but the on-call needs to know this changed, because the first time a hash join spills to disk someone will page us at midnight.
Rafael: Then that is mine. I own writing the runbook entry for the join strategy change, including how to override it per query.
Hana: Good.
Viktor: Also, my second monitor died this morning. It shows a green line down the middle and nothing else.
Rafael: There are spares in the cupboard by the printer, take one.
Viktor: I thought those were reserved for new starters.
Rafael: There are six of them, take one.
Hana: Okay. Planner change is mine, runbook is Rafael's. Both by the end of next week.
output: Kestrel will default to a hash join when both sides of a join are over ten million rows; Hana will make the planner change and test it against the slow query set. Rafael will write the runbook entry for the change, including the per-query override, and both are due by the end of next week.

input:
Ben: The new filter panel in Perch has been at ten percent of tenants for three weeks. Error rates are flat, support has not had a single complaint, and the two tenants who asked for it are happy.
Zoe: Ten to a hundred in one step is aggressive though. If there is a layout problem on a screen size we did not cover, we hear it from everyone at once.
Leila: Fifty is the usual next step. That is enough tenants that any remaining problem shows up, and few enough that it is not a crisis.
Ben: Fifty it is. I own moving the new filter panel flag to fifty percent of tenants tomorrow morning.
Zoe: And the release note? Tenants in the fifty will see a different panel with no explanation otherwise.
Leila: I will write it. Short, with a screenshot, linked from the panel itself. Leila owns the release note for the filter panel.
Ben: Thanks.
Zoe: I lost my house keys somewhere between the car park and here this morning. If anyone finds a ring with a small brass owl on it, it is mine.
Leila: Check reception, people hand things in there.
Zoe: I did. Nothing yet.
Ben: Ask the garage attendant too. Anyway, flag to fifty tomorrow, note is Leila's, done.
output: The Perch new filter panel flag moves from ten to fifty percent of tenants; Ben will make the change tomorrow morning. Leila will write the short release note for it, with a screenshot, linked from the panel itself.

input:
Elin: Every sprint someone adds a column to a Rookery core table and every sprint something downstream breaks because of it. Three incidents this quarter came from that.
Dario: The additions are all reasonable on their own. The problem is that nobody sees them together.
Kenji: A freeze would stop the bleeding. No schema changes to the core tables for the rest of the quarter, and anything urgent goes through a review with all three of us.
Elin: That is what I want to do. I own the freeze: I will announce it, add the check to the migration pipeline that rejects core table changes without the review label, and keep the exceptions list.
Dario: Customers who read the changelog will notice the schema section going quiet. We should say why.
Kenji: A one-paragraph note in the customer-facing changelog is enough. Dario, you own that note, this week.
Dario: Fine.
Kenji: Did anyone watch the match last night? Two goals in the last five minutes and I had already switched it off.
Elin: I saw the second one on my phone in the kitchen. Ridiculous.
Kenji: I am never switching off early again.
Elin: Okay. Freeze is mine, changelog note is Dario's. Let's move on.
output: Rookery's core tables are frozen for the rest of the quarter, with urgent changes going through a three-person review; Elin will announce the freeze, add the pipeline check for the review label, and keep the exceptions list. Dario will add a paragraph to the customer-facing changelog explaining the freeze this week.

input:
Kenji: Python 3.9 reached end of life months ago and keeping the SDK compatible with it is costing us. The typing syntax we want is 3.10 only, and the test matrix takes twenty minutes longer because of that one version.
Ana: How many customers still pin the SDK on 3.9?
Kenji: Download stats say under two percent, and most of those are CI images that have not been updated rather than real deployments.
Marcus: Two percent is small enough to drop with a warning in the release before the one that breaks.
Kenji: Agreed. I own dropping 3.9 support in the next release, with the deprecation warning going into the current release first.
Ana: And we need the build to refuse 3.9 rather than silently produce a wheel that half works. I will add the minimum version check to the CI pipeline and to the package metadata.
Kenji: Good. Ana owns the version check.
Marcus: There is cake in the kitchen, by the way. It is Ravi's birthday and his team ordered far too much.
Ana: What kind?
Marcus: Lemon, I think. Possibly carrot. It is orange.
Ana: I will investigate after this.
Kenji: Right. 3.9 drop is mine, CI check is Ana's, both in the next two releases.
output: The SDK will drop Python 3.9 support in the next release, with a deprecation warning in the current release first; Kenji owns the drop. Ana will add the minimum version check to the CI pipeline and the package metadata.

input:
Ravi: A tenant ran a query in Kestrel yesterday that returned four million rows to the browser. The tab crashed, they retried, and the second attempt took a worker for six minutes.
Mei: There is no cap on result size at all? I assumed there was.
Ravi: There is a cap on execution time, not on rows. A fast query that returns everything sails through.
Oscar: A hundred thousand rows is more than anyone can look at and less than what breaks a browser. Anything bigger should go through the export path, which streams.
Ravi: Then that is the number. I own capping Kestrel result sets at a hundred thousand rows, with a clear error that points at the export path.
Mei: The API users will hit that cap too and their code will not read the error message. The docs need a pagination section that explains the cap and shows the cursor parameter.
Oscar: Mei, can you own that docs section?
Mei: Yes, I will have it ready the same day the cap ships so nobody is surprised.
Oscar: I started cycling in this week. Forty minutes each way, and I have discovered that my building has nowhere to put a bike.
Ravi: The basement racks by the loading dock are free most days.
Oscar: I did not know those existed.
Ravi: Okay. Cap is mine, docs are Mei's, same day.
output: Kestrel result sets will be capped at a hundred thousand rows with an error that points at the streaming export path; Ravi will implement the cap. Mei will write the pagination section in the API docs explaining the cap and the cursor parameter, ready the same day the cap ships.

input:
Oscar: Talon notification mail is going out through the old provider and about four percent of it bounces. The new provider we already use for account mail bounces under one percent on the same domains.
Priya: Is there any difference in what Talon sends that would matter? Alert mail has a lot of links and some providers score that as spam.
Oscar: I sent a week of real alerts through the new provider from a staging tenant. Deliverability was fine.
Leila: Then there is no reason to wait. Oscar, you own migrating Talon notifications to the new mail provider, tenant by tenant over one week so a problem shows up small.
Oscar: Fine.
Priya: I want to see the bounce numbers after, not assume them. I will run the bounce-rate comparison for the week after the migration finishes and post it in the channel.
Leila: Good, Priya owns the bounce-rate check.
Oscar: Off topic, there is a podcast episode about how the shipping industry handles time zones and it is genuinely gripping. I will put the link in the channel.
Priya: Time zones are always a horror story.
Oscar: This one has a ship that arrived a day before it left.
Leila: Send it. Okay, migration is Oscar's, bounce check is Priya's, both done within the month.
output: Talon notification mail will move from the old provider to the new one that already serves account mail; Oscar will migrate it tenant by tenant over one week. Priya will run a bounce-rate comparison for the week after the migration finishes and post the numbers in the channel.

input:
Bruno: The load balancer marked two Magpie workers as healthy for an hour yesterday while they were wedged. It only checks that the port answers, and the port answered.
Felix: A real health endpoint would need to check the queue consumer is alive and the last batch finished within some window.
Amara: How long is the window? A worker that has been idle for an hour because there is nothing to do should not look unhealthy.
Bruno: Report unhealthy only if a batch is in progress and has been for more than ten minutes, or if the consumer thread is gone. Idle is fine.
Felix: That works. Bruno, you own the health endpoint on the Magpie workers with those two conditions.
Bruno: Yes.
Amara: And then the load balancer has to actually use it, which is a separate change in the infrastructure config. I will own wiring the new endpoint into the load balancer check once Bruno's endpoint is deployed.
Felix: Good, Amara owns the load balancer side.
Bruno: Whoever is nearest the printer on the third floor, it has been flashing a paper jam light since Monday and nobody has opened it.
Amara: I opened it. There is no paper in it. It is jammed on nothing.
Bruno: Then it is haunted.
Felix: I will file a ticket. Okay, endpoint is Bruno's, balancer wiring is Amara's.
output: Magpie workers get a real health endpoint that reports unhealthy when a batch has been in progress for more than ten minutes or the consumer thread is gone; Bruno will build it. Amara will wire the new endpoint into the load balancer check once it is deployed.

input:
Yara: The Rookery service credentials have not been rotated since the system went live. That is a finding waiting to happen in the next audit.
Marcus: Rotating them means every service that reads Rookery needs the new secret at roughly the same time, or it starts failing.
Yara: The secret store supports two active versions. We add the new one, roll the readers, then retire the old one. I have done it for the mail credentials already.
Ingrid: Then do it. Yara owns rotating the Rookery service credentials using the two-version method, this sprint.
Yara: Yes.
Marcus: And it needs to not be a one-off. Every ninety days, on the calendar, with a named owner, or we are back here in two years.
Ingrid: Marcus, you own adding the ninety-day rotation reminder to the team calendar and the runbook.
Marcus: Done by tomorrow.
Yara: Also, we are taking the new hire to lunch on Thursday. Anywhere but the noodle place, she has been three times this week already.
Ingrid: The sandwich place on the corner then.
Marcus: They close at two, so make it early.
Ingrid: Noted. Rotation is Yara's, reminder is Marcus's, moving on.
output: Yara will rotate the Rookery service credentials this sprint using the secret store's two-version method. Marcus will add a ninety-day rotation reminder with a named owner to the team calendar and the runbook by tomorrow.

input:
Nadia: Perch charts show every timestamp in UTC. A tenant in the far east opened a chart that said their traffic peaks at three in the morning, which it does not, it peaks at noon their time.
Jonas: The chart library supports a timezone on the date axis, we just never pass one.
Hana: Pass what, though? We do not store a timezone per tenant. We store a country, which is not the same thing.
Nadia: Then we need a timezone column in the tenant settings table, defaulting to UTC, editable in the admin screen.
Jonas: Two changes. The column and the admin screen, then the chart axis reads it.
Hana: I will take the column and the admin field. Hana owns adding the timezone setting to the tenant settings table and the admin screen.
Nadia: And I own switching the chart date axis to use the tenant timezone once the setting exists.
Jonas: Good.
Hana: I went hiking on Saturday, the ridge trail past the reservoir. Six hours, and I could not feel my legs on Sunday.
Nadia: Was that the one with the ladder section?
Hana: Yes. The ladder was fine, it was the descent afterwards.
Jonas: Okay. Column and admin field are Hana's, chart axis is Nadia's, in that order.
output: Perch charts will show timestamps in the tenant's timezone instead of UTC. Hana will add a timezone setting, defaulting to UTC, to the tenant settings table and the admin screen, and Nadia will then switch the chart date axis to use it.

input:
Priya: The Kestrel planner change went out this morning and the p95 latency on the reporting endpoint doubled within an hour. I want it rolled back tonight.
Tomasz: I can do that. Roll back the planner change at the end of the day, and we look at it again next week.
Priya: Okay, Tomasz owns the rollback tonight.
Lena: Hold on. I have been in the traces for the last hour and the slow requests are not spending their time in the planner. They are missing the result cache on every call.
Tomasz: Why would the planner change affect the cache?
Lena: It does not. The cache key includes the plan hash, and the new planner produces a different plan for the same query on every call because it includes a timestamp in the hash input. So every request is a cache miss. The plans themselves are fine, they are faster.
Priya: So if we roll back the planner we hide the problem, and the actual bug is the timestamp in the cache key.
Lena: Yes. Rolling back would also throw away the planner improvement, which is real.
Priya: Then scrap the rollback. Tomasz, do not roll back. Lena, you own fixing the cache key so the timestamp is not in the hash input, first thing tomorrow morning.
Lena: I can have it in review by ten.
Tomasz: Fine by me, I would rather not do a night deploy anyway. Also, whoever left a bag of oranges in the fridge, they are starting to ferment.
Priya: Not mine. Okay. No rollback, Lena fixes the cache key tomorrow.
output: The latency regression after the Kestrel planner change is caused by a timestamp in the cache key input that makes every request a cache miss, not by the planner itself, so the rollback Tomasz was going to do tonight is cancelled. Lena will fix the cache key to exclude the timestamp first thing tomorrow morning.

input:
Sofia: Magpie throughput is the bottleneck for the big tenant's backfill. We batch at a thousand rows and I want to raise it to five thousand, which in my local test was almost four times faster.
Dev: It should be, the per-batch overhead is most of the cost at a thousand.
Sofia: Then I own raising the batch size to five thousand, today.
Amara: Which workers did you test on?
Sofia: My laptop, so effectively unlimited memory.
Amara: The production workers are the small class with two gigabytes. A five thousand row batch of the wide events is about three gigabytes decoded. It will not fit. The worker will be killed and the batch retried forever.
Dev: She is right, I have seen that exact loop with the old importer.
Sofia: Then five thousand is off the table on the current workers. What do we do instead?
Dev: Keep the batch at a thousand and add a second worker pool. Twice the workers gives most of the throughput without touching memory per worker, and we can turn it off after the backfill.
Sofia: Okay, forget the batch size change. Batch stays at a thousand. Dev, you own adding the second worker pool for the backfill period.
Dev: I will have it running by tomorrow afternoon.
Amara: Reminder that the fire drill is at eleven and we are supposed to actually leave the building this time.
Sofia: Noted. Batch size unchanged, second pool is Dev's.
output: Raising the Magpie batch size from a thousand to five thousand is dropped because the batches would not fit in the production workers' memory, so the batch size stays at a thousand. Dev will add a second worker pool for the backfill period instead, running by tomorrow afternoon.

input:
Ben: The Perch export is corrupting files for some tenants, columns shifted by one from a certain point down. Until we understand it, I want the export disabled for everyone.
Zoe: Everyone? Hundreds of tenants export every morning and most of those files are fine.
Ben: A silently wrong file is worse than no file. Disable it for all tenants, I will own the switch, and we turn it back on when the fix is in.
Leila: Before you do, I pulled the reports. Every corrupted file came from a tenant with more than fifty columns in the export. Not one from under fifty.
Ben: All of them?
Leila: All eleven. The column shift starts at column fifty-one every time, which looks like a buffer boundary in the writer.
Zoe: Then disabling it for everyone is punishing the ninety percent who are not affected.
Ben: Fair. Change of plan. Do not disable the export globally. Instead, block the export only when the column count is over fifty, with a message saying we are fixing it.
Zoe: I can add that guard today, it is one check in the export handler. Zoe owns the column-count guard.
Ben: And I will take the actual writer bug separately once we confirm the boundary theory.
Leila: Does anyone know why the fourth floor smells of paint? Nobody told us about any work up there.
Ben: The meeting rooms are being redone. Okay, guard over fifty columns, Zoe, today.
output: The Perch export corruption only affects tenants with more than fifty columns, so the plan to disable the export for all tenants is dropped. Zoe will add a guard today that blocks the export only when the column count is over fifty, with a message saying a fix is under way, while Ben investigates the writer bug.

input:
Hana: The Tuesday release keeps colliding with the Monday planning meeting, so half the changes are merged in a rush on Monday evening. I want to move the weekly release to Thursday.
Viktor: Thursday gives two more days of merging and a calmer Monday.
Hana: Then I own moving the release day to Thursday from next week. Viktor, tell the support leads.
Rafael: One thing. If a Thursday release goes wrong, the fix lands Friday, and if the Friday fix goes wrong, we are into the weekend. Tuesday was chosen so a bad release has three working days of runway.
Viktor: That was the original reason, yes. I had forgotten.
Hana: I had not thought about the weekend at all. That is a real problem, especially with the on-call change.
Rafael: The rush on Monday evening is the actual complaint. That can be solved without moving the release. Add a Friday hotfix window so small fixes do not have to squeeze into Monday, and keep the release on Tuesday.
Hana: Okay, I am reversing myself. The release stays on Tuesday. Viktor, you own setting up the Friday hotfix window with a written scope for what qualifies.
Viktor: Small, reviewed, no schema changes. I will write it down today.
Hana: Good.
Rafael: Also, the vending machine on two now takes cards. I found out by accident.
Hana: Progress. Right, Tuesday stays, Friday hotfix window is Viktor's.
output: The weekly release stays on Tuesday after all, because a Thursday release would leave a bad release with no runway before the weekend. Instead Viktor will set up a Friday hotfix window with a written scope, limited to small reviewed changes with no schema changes.

input:
Kenji: The legacy v1 branch of the SDK has not had a commit in two years and it confuses every new contributor who clones the repository. I want to delete it.
Ana: Nobody is building from it, as far as I know.
Kenji: Then I own deleting the v1 branch this week.
Marcus: Before you delete it, two of the oldest customers are still on v1 in production. If they hit a security issue we would need to cut a patch from that branch. A tag is not enough, the release scripts expect a branch.
Ana: Could we recreate it from the tag if that ever happened?
Marcus: Yes, but the person doing it at two in the morning would not know the tag name, and the branch protection rules and CI config are attached to the branch, not the tag.
Kenji: Fine, deletion is off. But I still do not want it in the default branch list confusing people.
Ana: Archive it. Mark the branch read-only, add a note in the readme pointing at it, and hide it from the default listing. Nothing is lost and nobody trips over it.
Kenji: That works. So, not deleted. Ana, you own archiving the v1 branch as read-only with the readme note.
Ana: Today.
Marcus: On a lighter note, the window by my desk now opens. Facilities fixed it after only fourteen months.
Kenji: A miracle. Okay, v1 branch archived, Ana has it.
output: The SDK's legacy v1 branch will not be deleted after all, because two customers still run v1 in production and a security patch might need to be cut from it. Ana will archive the branch as read-only, hide it from the default listing, and add a readme note pointing at it, today.

input:
Ravi: The Talon daily digest is used by about a fifth of tenants and everyone who uses it loves it. I think we should turn it on by default for everyone.
Mei: It is a good feature. Turning it on by default is a lot more people seeing it.
Ravi: Then I own switching the digest to on by default in the next release.
Oscar: I need to push back on that. Support has had complaints from tenants who did not ask for the digest and got one because an admin enabled it by mistake. Unasked-for mail is how we end up on spam lists, and the alert mail rides on the same domain.
Mei: That is the same domain the critical alerts use?
Oscar: Same domain, same sending address. One bad reputation score and critical alerts start landing in spam folders.
Ravi: I did not know they shared a domain. That changes it. Okay, the digest stays opt-in. Forget the default change.
Mei: But we can still get more people to find it. An in-app banner on the alerts page, shown once, pointing at the digest setting. No mail involved.
Ravi: Good. Mei, you own the one-time in-app banner promoting the digest.
Mei: Next release.
Oscar: Thanks. Also, if anyone has a spare charger for the older laptop model, mine has decided to only work at a specific angle.
Ravi: Check the drawer by reception. Okay, digest stays opt-in, banner is Mei's.
output: The Talon daily digest stays opt-in rather than being turned on by default, because unasked-for digest mail could damage the sending domain that critical alerts share. Mei will add a one-time in-app banner on the alerts page promoting the digest setting in the next release.

input:
Oscar: The Rookery backups still go to the old bucket, which is in the region we are leaving. I want to move them to the new bucket this week so the old region can be closed.
Priya: Is the new bucket ready?
Oscar: Policies, encryption, lifecycle rules, all in place. It is a config change on the backup job and a one-time copy of the existing snapshots.
Priya: Then do it. Oscar owns moving the backups to the new bucket this week.
Ingrid: I am sorry to be that person, but the audit freeze started Monday. No changes to backup locations, retention, or access until the auditors sign off, which is the end of the month at the earliest. It is in the freeze notice.
Oscar: I read the notice and I did not connect backups to it.
Ingrid: It names backup storage explicitly, because last year's finding was about exactly that.
Priya: Then we cannot do it this week, and I would rather not ask for an exemption over something that can wait three weeks.
Oscar: Agreed. The old region costs us a few hundred a month, it is not urgent.
Priya: So the backup move is deferred until the audit closes. I own adding it to the post-audit list with Oscar as the person who picks it up.
Ingrid: Thank you.
Oscar: Unrelated, the kitchen has run out of the good tea again and it has only been four days.
Priya: Buy two boxes next time. Okay, backups wait for the audit, list update is mine.
output: Moving the Rookery backups to the new bucket this week is cancelled because the audit freeze forbids changes to backup storage until the auditors sign off. The move is deferred until the audit closes, and Priya will add it to the post-audit list with Oscar as the person who picks it up.

input:
Bruno: The Perch search box feels sluggish. Every keystroke fires a request and the results flicker. I want a two hundred millisecond debounce on the client so we send one request per pause instead of one per key.
Felix: That is a standard fix, and cheap.
Bruno: Then I own adding the debounce this sprint.
Yara: Can I show you something first? I profiled the search endpoint yesterday. The median response is eight hundred milliseconds, and almost all of it is the database, because the search column has no index and every query scans the whole table.
Felix: Eight hundred on the server? A debounce would not fix that, it would just send fewer slow requests.
Yara: Right. The flicker is the slow responses arriving out of order, not the request volume. Add the index and the responses come back in under fifty milliseconds and the flicker disappears, no client change needed.
Bruno: I assumed it was the volume. If it is the index, then the debounce is treating the wrong thing.
Felix: I will own adding the index on the search column. It is a migration on a medium table, so I will run it during the low-traffic window on Wednesday.
Bruno: Okay, no debounce. Felix owns the index. If it still flickers after that we talk again.
Yara: It will not.
Felix: By the way, the standing desk in the corner is free now that Dario moved floors, if anyone wants it.
Bruno: Tempting. Right, index on Wednesday, Felix.
output: The Perch search sluggishness is caused by a missing index on the search column making every query scan the whole table, not by request volume, so the client-side debounce Bruno proposed is dropped. Felix will add the index on the search column during the low-traffic window on Wednesday.

input:
Yara: Kestrel allows twenty concurrent queries per tenant and one tenant is using all twenty around the clock, starving everyone else on the shared pool. I want to cut the limit to ten.
Marcus: Ten would halve their footprint immediately.
Yara: Then I own cutting the per-tenant concurrency limit from twenty to ten in tomorrow's config release.
Nadia: Which tenant is it?
Yara: The logistics customer, the one on the annual contract.
Nadia: Their contract specifies twenty concurrent queries. It is in the order form, I negotiated it. Cutting them to ten would be a breach, and their dashboards genuinely run twenty parallel panels.
Marcus: So the limit is not the problem, it is that they share a pool with everyone else.
Nadia: Exactly. They are using what they paid for.
Yara: Okay, then I am withdrawing the cut. The limit stays at twenty. What we need is a way to give that tenant their own capacity without letting them eat the shared pool.
Marcus: A per-tenant pool override. Tenants with a contracted limit get their own worker pool sized to it, everyone else stays on the shared pool. I own adding the per-tenant pool override to Kestrel this sprint.
Yara: Good. Nadia, send Marcus the list of tenants with contracted limits.
Nadia: Sure. Also, the good meeting room has a new projector and it actually turns on in under a minute now.
Yara: Finally. Okay, limit stays at twenty, Marcus owns the pool override.
output: The per-tenant Kestrel concurrency limit stays at twenty, because the tenant using all twenty has that number in their contract, so the cut to ten is withdrawn. Marcus will add a per-tenant worker pool override this sprint so tenants with contracted limits get their own capacity instead of the shared pool.

input:
Nadia: Magpie's JSON parsing is about a third of ingest CPU. The new parsing library claims to be five times faster on the benchmarks I have seen. I want to switch to it.
Jonas: A third of CPU is a lot. If the claim is half true it is worth it.
Nadia: Then I own switching the parser in Magpie to the new library this sprint.
Hana: I actually tried it last week on our real event samples, not the published benchmarks. On our payloads it was about the same speed, because most of our events are small and the new library's advantage is on large documents. And it rejects two of our tenants' events outright, they use a duplicate key pattern the strict parser refuses.
Jonas: Same speed and it breaks two tenants?
Hana: Same speed within noise. The rejections are the real problem, the old parser takes the last value and those tenants depend on that.
Nadia: That is not what I expected at all. If it does not help on our payloads there is no reason to take the risk. Cancel the switch, we stay on the current parser.
Hana: The duplicate key rejection is arguably a bug in the new library, since the spec allows an implementation to accept it. Somebody should tell them.
Jonas: I will own filing the upstream report with our sample events, so if we revisit this in a year the problem is known.
Nadia: Good. Also, somebody has been leaving the balcony door open and the corridor is freezing.
Jonas: Not me. Okay, parser stays, upstream report is mine.
output: Magpie stays on its current JSON parser, because the new library was no faster on real event payloads and rejects the duplicate key pattern two tenants depend on, so the planned switch is cancelled. Jonas will file an upstream report about the duplicate key rejection with sample events.

input:
Priya: Two things today, ingest lag and dashboard load time, and they are tangled because the same tenants complain about both.
Tomasz: On ingest, lag is climbing during the European morning because four Magpie workers cannot keep up with the new tenant's volume. Eight workers would clear the queue in under ten minutes.
Lena: On dashboards, the first load of the day takes fifteen seconds because the cache is cold. It is not lag, the data is there, it is just not cached.
Priya: Let's take ingest first. Tomasz, is eight workers a config change or a capacity request?
Tomasz: Config. The instance pool has room. I own raising the Magpie worker count from four to eight tomorrow morning.
Priya: Good. Now while we are on performance, I keep wondering whether Perch should move to server-side rendering. It would make first paint faster everywhere.
Lena: It would also be a quarter of work and touch every screen. That is a roadmap conversation, not a Tuesday one.
Priya: Agreed, park it. Nobody is deciding on server-side rendering today. Back to dashboards.
Lena: The cold cache is fixable now. Warm the cache for the twenty most-viewed dashboards at five in the morning, before anyone logs in. It is a scheduled job calling the existing endpoints.
Priya: Do it. Lena owns cache warming for the top twenty dashboards, scheduled at five.
Tomasz: One more on ingest, the new tenant also sends a burst at midnight their time, which is the same window. Eight workers still covers it, I checked the numbers.
Priya: Fine. Anyone want the last of the pastries from the client meeting? They are in the kitchen.
Lena: Taking two. So: workers to eight, Tomasz; cache warming, Lena; rendering parked.
output: Tomasz will raise the Magpie worker count from four to eight tomorrow morning to clear the European-morning ingest lag from the new tenant's volume. Lena will add a scheduled job at five in the morning that warms the cache for the twenty most-viewed Perch dashboards. Moving Perch to server-side rendering was raised but explicitly parked with no decision.

input:
Kenji: We have the SDK release and the docs site on the agenda, and they overlap because the docs are built from the SDK repository.
Ana: The docs build has been broken on the old pipeline for a week. The new pipeline builds it fine but nothing is pointed at it yet.
Marcus: And the SDK 2.4 release is waiting on the docs, because we do not ship a release whose docs page is a build error.
Kenji: Then the docs pipeline goes first. Ana, you own moving the docs build to the new pipeline and pointing the docs site at its output. When?
Ana: Wednesday.
Kenji: Then 2.4 can go Friday. I own cutting the SDK 2.4 release on Friday, assuming docs are green on Wednesday.
Marcus: While we are talking about the release, should we rename the package? The current name is nothing like the product name and every new user searches for the wrong thing.
Ana: A rename is a migration for every existing user. It is not a 2.4 thing.
Kenji: Not a 2.4 thing and not a decision for today. I would want a written proposal with the deprecation plan before anyone even votes. Park the rename.
Marcus: Fair.
Ana: Back to docs for a second. The new pipeline also builds the changelog page, so 2.4 will have a proper changelog for the first time.
Kenji: Good, that makes Friday easier.
Marcus: Is anyone else's badge photo now ten years old on the new directory page? Mine has hair.
Ana: Mine has a fringe I deeply regret.
Kenji: Okay. Docs to the new pipeline Wednesday, Ana; 2.4 on Friday, me; rename parked.
output: Ana will move the docs build to the new pipeline and point the docs site at its output by Wednesday, and Kenji will then cut the SDK 2.4 release on Friday once the docs are green. Renaming the SDK package was raised but explicitly parked pending a written proposal.

input:
Dev: Alert noise and the on-call handover are both on the list. They are related, because most of the handover is spent explaining which alerts to ignore.
Sofia: On handover, we have no template. Each person writes whatever they remember, and last week an open incident was left out entirely.
Dev: On noise, the disk alert fires at eighty percent and every server sits at eighty-five all week by design. It is forty pages a week that mean nothing.
Priya: Take noise first. What is the right threshold?
Dev: Ninety. Nothing has ever actually filled up below ninety-two, and ninety leaves a day of warning. I own raising the disk alert threshold to ninety percent this week.
Priya: Good. Now on the handover, Sofia, what does the template need?
Sofia: Open incidents with status, alerts silenced and why, and anything scheduled in the next shift. One page. I will own writing the handover template and putting it in the on-call channel pinned message.
Priya: Done. Sofia has the template.
Dev: While we are on paging, should we finally pay for a proper paging tool instead of the mail-and-phone setup? Everyone I talk to uses one.
Priya: Maybe, but that is a budget item with a per-seat cost, and budgeting is next month. Bring it there, we are not deciding a purchase in this meeting.
Dev: Fine, next month.
Sofia: One more on noise, the handover template should have a line for alerts that were raised to a new threshold this shift, so people know the disk one moved.
Dev: Good idea, add it.
Priya: Also, the lift on the north side is out again, use the south one. Okay, disk to ninety is Dev's, template is Sofia's, paging tool goes to budgeting.
output: Dev will raise the disk alert threshold from eighty to ninety percent this week to cut the pages that mean nothing. Sofia will write a one-page on-call handover template covering open incidents, silenced alerts, scheduled work, and threshold changes, and pin it in the on-call channel. Buying a dedicated paging tool was raised but deferred to next month's budgeting, with no decision today.

input:
Amara: Rookery cost and the escalation from the retail customer are both on today. They touch because the escalation is about a query that costs us a fortune to run.
Ingrid: The customer first. They had a wrong number on their board report on Friday and their CFO noticed before we did. They want a written root cause, and they want it this week.
Amara: On cost, sixty percent of storage is partitions nobody has queried in six months. Moving those to the cold tier saves about a third of the bill and they stay queryable, just slower.
Ravi: Slower by how much?
Amara: First query on a cold partition takes a couple of minutes to rehydrate, then it is normal. For six-month-old data that is acceptable.
Ingrid: Do it, but not the retail customer's partitions until their escalation is closed, we do not want a slow query in the middle of a root cause conversation.
Amara: Agreed. I own moving cold partitions to the cheaper tier, excluding that customer until Ingrid says so.
Ravi: On the escalation, the wrong number was a late-arriving batch that was counted in the wrong day. It is understood. The write-up is the work.
Ingrid: I own sending the customer the written root cause by Wednesday, with the fix and the date it shipped.
Ravi: Should we look at switching warehouse vendor? The cost conversation comes up every quarter.
Amara: We looked last year. A migration would cost more than three years of the savings. Not on the table, and I do not want to reopen it.
Ingrid: Agreed, no vendor change.
Ravi: Someone left a very nice umbrella in the big meeting room, if it is yours.
Amara: Not mine. Okay: cold tier is mine, root cause by Wednesday is Ingrid's, vendor stays.
output: Amara will move Rookery partitions unqueried for six months to the cheaper cold tier, excluding the retail customer's partitions until their escalation is closed. Ingrid will send that customer a written root cause for the miscounted late batch by Wednesday, including the fix and its ship date. Switching warehouse vendor was raised and explicitly rejected.

input:
Rafael: Two items, the planner regression and the hiring loop. Both need an owner today.
Hana: On the planner, the regression was a join reorder that made one class of query ten times slower, and we found it because a customer told us. Nothing in CI would have caught it.
Rafael: What would catch it?
Hana: A regression suite of the thirty slowest real queries, anonymised, run against the planner on every merge, failing if any plan cost goes up by more than double. I own adding that planner regression check to CI this sprint.
Rafael: Good. On hiring, Viktor, what is the problem with the loop?
Viktor: We have no round that checks whether someone can design a system. We check coding and we check behaviour, and then we hire people who can write a function but cannot lay out a service.
Rafael: Add a round?
Viktor: A one-hour systems design round, same prompt for every candidate, two interviewers. I own adding it to the loop and writing the interviewer guide before the next candidate, which is in two weeks.
Hana: While we are on the planner, someone will suggest rewriting it in a faster language. Can we not?
Rafael: Nobody is rewriting the planner. It is not the language, it is the cost model. That is not a decision, it is a joke, and it stays one.
Hana: Thank you.
Viktor: Also on hiring, the systems round replaces nothing, the loop gets longer by an hour. Candidates should be told.
Rafael: Put it in the scheduling mail. Anyone else find the new keyboard trays wobble?
Hana: Mine is fine, tighten the screws underneath. Okay: planner regression check is Hana's, systems design round is Viktor's, no rewrite.
output: Hana will add a planner regression check to CI this sprint that runs the thirty slowest anonymised real queries on every merge and fails if any plan cost more than doubles. Viktor will add a one-hour systems design round with two interviewers to the hiring loop and write the interviewer guide before the next candidate in two weeks. Rewriting the planner in another language was mentioned and dismissed, not decided.

input:
Leila: Accessibility and tenant onboarding today. The same customer complained about both.
Theo: On onboarding, provisioning a new tenant is still a twelve-step manual checklist and it takes a day. Last week a step was skipped and the tenant had no alerting for three days.
Leila: On accessibility, the filter chips in Perch fail the contrast check. Grey text on light grey. A customer's audit flagged it and they cannot roll out the product to their staff until it passes.
Ben: The contrast is a token change in the design system plus a check that it does not break the dark theme.
Leila: Then I own fixing the contrast on the filter chips, both themes, this week.
Theo: Onboarding is a script. Every step is already a command someone runs by hand, they just need to be one command with checks between them. I own automating the tenant provisioning script so the checklist becomes one run.
Leila: Good. While we are on the audit, they also asked when we drop support for the old browser, because their accessibility tooling does not work on it.
Ben: We could drop it. Usage is under one percent.
Leila: We could, but two large tenants are locked to it by their IT departments. That is a decision with a customer conversation attached and it is not for today. Note it, no decision.
Theo: Fine. Back on onboarding, once the script exists the turnaround becomes an hour, so sales can promise same-day setup, but only after it works.
Leila: After it works.
Ben: The office is doing a plant sale on Friday, apparently. I do not know why.
Theo: Neither do I. Okay: chips contrast is Leila's, provisioning script is Theo's, old browser undecided.
output: Leila will fix the contrast on the Perch filter chips in both themes this week so the customer's accessibility audit passes. Theo will automate the twelve-step tenant provisioning checklist into a single script with checks between steps. Dropping support for the old browser was raised but left undecided pending a customer conversation.

input:
Bruno: Schema drift in Magpie and the quarterly planning date. Two subjects, one meeting, let's be quick.
Elin: On planning, we need a date for the offsite before the venue fills. I have three options, all in the last week of the quarter.
Bruno: On drift, a tenant changed a field from a string to an object last week and the ingest happily wrote nonsense into that column for two days. We only found it because a dashboard went blank.
Felix: Nothing checks the incoming shape against the last known shape?
Bruno: Nothing. Every field is accepted as whatever arrives.
Felix: Then we need drift detection: record the shape per tenant, compare each batch, and quarantine the batch with an alert if a type changes.
Bruno: That is what I want to build. I own adding schema drift detection to the Magpie ingest, with quarantine and a Talon alert, this sprint.
Elin: Back to planning. Of the three dates, the Thursday works for everyone but one person, and that person said they could dial in for the morning.
Bruno: Book the Thursday. Elin owns booking the planning offsite for that date.
Elin: Done today.
Felix: One suggestion on drift. While the detection is being built, should we freeze all ingest changes so nothing else moves under us?
Bruno: No. Two other teams have ingest changes landing this sprint that have nothing to do with drift, and a freeze would block them for no benefit. Detection ships alongside them. Rejected.
Felix: Okay, withdrawn.
Elin: The offsite venue has a climbing wall, by the way, so bring shoes you can climb in.
Bruno: I will bring shoes I can sit in. Okay: drift detection is mine, offsite booking is Elin's, no freeze.
output: Bruno will add schema drift detection to the Magpie ingest this sprint, recording each tenant's field shapes, quarantining any batch whose types change, and raising a Talon alert. Elin will book the quarterly planning offsite for the Thursday that works for everyone today. Freezing all ingest changes while detection is built was proposed and rejected.

input:
Kofi: API versioning and the security review, which meet because the review wants v2 in scope.
Yara: On the review, the external pen test has to happen this half. October is the only slot the firm has left, and they need scope agreed a month ahead.
Kofi: On versioning, the v2 metrics API is finished. The question is how to ship it without breaking every v1 caller.
Viktor: Header-selected. Callers send a version header, default is v1, v2 only when asked for. No URL change, no breakage.
Kofi: That is the plan. I own shipping the v2 metrics API behind a version header, defaulting to v1, next release.
Yara: And the pen test should cover v2, so it needs to be live in staging by September. Does that work?
Kofi: It will be in staging next week, so yes.
Yara: Then I own scheduling the pen test for October with the firm and sending them the scope, including v2, by the end of this month.
Viktor: If v2 is better, why keep v1 at all? Sunset it at the same time and be done.
Kofi: Because every integration in the field calls v1 and none of them send a version header. Sunsetting v1 now would break all of them on the same day. Not agreed, and not a decision for this meeting. A sunset needs its own timeline.
Viktor: Okay, I withdraw it.
Yara: One thing on the review, the firm asked for a contact during the test. Kofi, that is you, unless you object.
Kofi: I do not object.
Viktor: The air conditioning in the small room is stuck on arctic, so bring a jacket if you book it.
Yara: Noted. So: v2 behind a header is Kofi's, pen test in October is mine, v1 stays.
output: Kofi will ship the v2 metrics API in the next release behind a version header that defaults to v1, so existing callers are unaffected, and will be the firm's contact during the test. Yara will schedule the external pen test for October and send the scope, including v2, by the end of this month. Sunsetting v1 immediately was proposed and not agreed.

input:
Oscar: Talon SMS and audit-log retention. The second one has a deadline.
Amara: Retention first, then. The compliance review asks for one year of audit logs and we keep ninety days. We have until the end of next month to be compliant.
Oscar: On SMS, we send a text for every severity, and low-severity alerts at three in the morning are the top complaint in the last survey. People are muting the number and then missing the critical ones.
Nadia: So the low-severity texts are actively harmful, they cause the muting.
Oscar: Exactly. I own disabling SMS for anything below critical severity. Those still go by mail and in-app, only the text stops. Next release.
Amara: Back to retention. Extending audit logs to a year is a config change on the retention policy plus a storage bump, which I have already priced and it is small. I own extending audit-log retention to one year before the compliance deadline.
Nadia: Do the logs older than ninety days still exist, or are they gone?
Amara: Gone. Retention starts accruing from now, and the review accepts that with a written note, which I will include.
Nadia: On SMS, should we sign up a second provider for redundancy? The current one had that outage in spring.
Oscar: One outage in two years, and a second provider doubles the integration surface and the monthly minimum. No. We are not adding a second provider.
Nadia: Fine.
Amara: One more on SMS: the critical texts should say critical in the first word, so anyone who did mute the number and looks later sees it immediately.
Oscar: Good, I will include that.
Nadia: Also, the lost property box at reception is overflowing. Okay: SMS below critical off is Oscar's, one-year retention is Amara's, no second provider.
output: Oscar will disable Talon SMS for all alerts below critical severity in the next release, leaving mail and in-app delivery unchanged and putting the word critical first in the texts that remain. Amara will extend audit-log retention from ninety days to one year before the compliance deadline at the end of next month, with a written note that the extension accrues from now. Adding a second SMS provider was proposed and rejected.

input:
Marcus: Query caching in Kestrel and the release checklist. Both have waited three weeks.
Zoe: The checklist first, because it is small. The last two bad releases were rolled back late because nobody knew who was allowed to call the rollback or how. It is not written anywhere.
Marcus: On caching, result caching has been behind a flag for a month. For read-only tenants, who only load dashboards and never write through the API, it cuts median latency by two thirds with no staleness risk.
Ravi: And for tenants who write?
Marcus: For writers the cache can serve a stale result for up to a minute after a write, which some of them would not accept. So not for them, not yet.
